intro: When you search for the best divorce advice near me, you are likely looking for clear, local guidance on the divorce process, finances, and children arrangements. You want to understand your options before making decisions, and you may be unsure who to turn to for reliable early advice.
need_heading: What people searching for divorce advice usually need
need_lead: Most people want to understand the legal and financial implications of divorce before they commit to a course of action.
needs: You want to know how the divorce process works in England or Wales, including the steps and what is expected of you.
You are concerned about how finances will be divided and want advice on protecting your position.
You need guidance on arrangements for children, including where they will live and how much time they will spend with each parent.
You are considering mediation or collaborative law and want to know if these options suit your situation.
You want to speak to a solicitor near you who can explain the law clearly and help you make informed choices.
context_heading: Understanding regulation and finding the right help
context: Solicitors in England and Wales are regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA), and you can check an individual or firm on the SRA's register. In Scotland, solicitors are regulated by the Law Society of Scotland, and in Northern Ireland by the Law Society of Northern Ireland. Regulated firms must hold professional indemnity insurance and have a complaints procedure; if that does not resolve things, the Legal Ombudsman can look at service complaints in England and Wales.

The word "lawyer" is not protected on its own, so check that whoever handles your matter is a solicitor, a chartered legal executive (CILEx) or another authorised professional. Reserved activities such as conducting court litigation and certain probate and conveyancing work can only be carried out by authorised people.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Mention that you are looking for divorce advice and whether you have already started proceedings.
Explain briefly what you hope to achieve, such as understanding the process, sorting out finances, or arranging children matters.
Say whether you are in England, Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland, as the law and regulation differ.
Let us know if you are interested in mediation or collaborative approaches.
Include your preferred way of being contacted and any times you are available.
Mention any particular concerns you have, such as protecting assets or dealing with a difficult conversation with your ex-partner.
questions: What are the first steps I need to take if I want to start a divorce?
How will my finances be assessed and what information will I need to provide?
What are my options for arranging children's living and contact arrangements?
Would mediation or collaborative law be suitable for my situation?
How do you charge for your services and what might the total cost be?
Are you regulated by the SRA (or the relevant body in my country) and what is your complaints procedure?

faqs.q: How do I know if a divorce adviser is properly qualified?
faqs.a: Check that they are a solicitor, chartered legal executive, or otherwise authorised. In England and Wales, you can verify a solicitor on the SRA register. Regulated firms must have professional indemnity insurance and a complaints procedure.

faqs.q: Can iComply recommend the best divorce solicitor for me?
faqs.a: iComply introduces you to a suitable professional based on your needs, but we do not rank or endorse anyone as best. You should ask questions and check credentials to decide who is right for you.

faqs.q: What should I prepare before speaking to a divorce solicitor?
faqs.a: Gather basic information about your finances, such as income, assets, and debts, and think about what you want to achieve. It also helps to note key dates and any concerns about children.

faqs.q: Is divorce advice different in Scotland or Northern Ireland?
faqs.a: Yes, the legal system and regulators differ. In Scotland, solicitors are regulated by the Law Society of Scotland; in Northern Ireland, by the Law Society of Northern Ireland. Always check that your adviser is regulated in the country where you live.
